1608.prule: Lexically contrastive word prosody of the Philippine type: minimal pairs distinguish penult-prominent from ultima-prominent words (French: gútum 'famine' vs gutúm 'to be hungry', báguy vs bagúy; Rappa: pũnu' 'tree' vs punu' 'full', ãbut 'catch' vs abut 'arrive'). French labels the contrast phonemic stress; Rappa labels the same contrast phonemic penultimate vowel length and then calls 'stress' predictable penultimate (secondary on the prepenult, ultima at sentence end), while conceding that length and stress cannot be told apart except by meaning contrast. Either way prominence position is not computable from syllable count.
1608.srule: Rappa 1996 sec. 3: secondary stress on the prepenultimate (antepenult) syllable of every word of more than two syllables, kept there under suffixation ('primary stress on the penultimate and secondary stress on the prepenultimate'). French c.1979 sec. 5 (stress group): a secondary stress is required when more than three syllables precede the primary, and a syllable may carry secondary stress when one syllable separates it from the primary; tertiary stress two syllables before the secondary ([ma̋duyúm] 'dark', [pʰɩna̋kʌma̋duyúm] 'darkest', [k̋ʌbʌbaiíhan] 'a group of women that were counted'). The two sources disagree on placement (adjacent to the primary vs one syllable removed).

1609.dq: According to such an analysis, word stress in Rotokas is a fixed system in the sense that the location of stress is predictable by general rules. Furthermore, it appears to be governed purely by phonological factors (distance from word edges, syllable weight, etc.) and not by morphological factors such as the distinction between roots and suffixes.
1609.heavy: Heavy = syllable with a long vowel (Robinson Tables 3.9-3.11: rii, pii, kee, taa H vs ke, pa, to, ro L; 'a foot consists of either a heavy syllable or two light syllables', sec. 3.2.3); syllables are (C)V with no codas. All nineteen words in Robinson's Table 3.8 ('Bisyllabic Words Stressed on the Second Syllable', p. 32) have a short first vowel and a long, stressed second vowel (kapóː, kapúː, ketóː, kokéː, kokóː, kopíː, koróː, kupíː, kuróː, kusíː, repóː, roróː, rugóː, tavóː, tokíː, toríː, turáː, visíː, voróː). The weight of unlike-vowel sequences is left open: for po.po.te.pai.ra.ra Robinson flags the ai sequence as a complication, and 'The treatment of vowel sequences remains an issue for more in-depth investigation' (sec. 3.2.1). Firchow 1973 says only that long vowels 'complicate' the count rules.
1609.dflt: Initial primary in all-light words per both sources for 2-4 syllables (10, 100, 1010 with sigma3 secondary per Firchow/Robinson); for all-light words of 5+ syllables the sources part: Firchow 1973 puts the strongest stress on the antepenult (garu'tuvira = 00100), Robinson's leftmost-foot rule predicts initial primary with antepenult secondary (10100) and calls Firchow's claim 'questionable'.
1609.prule: Firchow et al. 1973 ('Simplified rules of stress'): 2-3 syllables -> first syllable stressed; 4 syllables -> first and third; 5+ syllables -> 'the third from the last syllable is stressed most strongly' (garu'tuvira, popote'pairara); the rules 'are complicated by the occurrence of long vowels' and rule 3 fails 'in some longer verb constructions'. Robinson 2011 reanalysis: quantity-sensitive trochaic feet built left to right (heavy = long-vowel syllable), primary stress on the head of the leftmost proper foot, secondary on later foot heads, degenerate feet unstressed; net primary = initial, except peninitial when the word begins Light+Heavy (to'rii, ka'po:, Table 3.8). Robinson calls Firchow's antepenult-primary claim for 5+ syllable words 'questionable' but gives no long-word data of his own, so primary placement in words of 5+ syllables is unresolved between the two sources.
1609.srule: Robinson 2011 (sec. 3.2.2, p. 32): with quantity-sensitive trochaic feet parsed left to right (proper foot = one long-vowel syllable or two light syllables), secondary stress falls on the first syllable of every foot after the first; degenerate feet (a stray light syllable) are unstressed. Matches Firchow et al. 1973's count statement that 4-syllable words stress 'the first and third syllables' (etokasi, atarito) and that in 5+-syllable words the antepenult is stressed 'most strongly' (other stresses weaker; which of the two is primary in long all-light words is unresolved between the sources, see primary rule).

1614.heavy: In Sabanê, heavy syllables are those that have a coda. The coda position can only be filled by glides, a coronal nasal consonant, or a glottal stop.
1614.prule: Primary stress on the rightmost heavy (closed) syllable of the root; if the root has no heavy syllable, on the penultimate syllable. Heavy syllables may be stressed word-finally. Summary p. 226: binary left-headed feet built right-to-left from the primary.

1615.prule: Accent invariably on the penultimate syllable; under suffixation the accent moves so as to remain penultimate (quantity-insensitive, counted from the right edge).
1615.srule: No secondary stress is described (Wray speaks of a single 'accent' per word). 1615.tone: Wray 1894 speaks only of 'accent' (penultimate) and never mentions tone. A modern description WAS reached in Stage B: Breteler 2018 (LOT 502, ch.2 'Saghala tone', pp.26-31, data from Patin 2002, 2009 'Tone shift and tone spread in the Saghala noun phrase', Faits de Langues - Les Cahiers 1:229-244 per Breteler's bibliography) treats Saghala (Guthrie E74b) as a restricted/privative tone ('pitch-accent'-like) system: "The case at hand is the tonology of noun phrases in Saghala (Guthrie's E74b), spoken in southeastern Kenya.... Further following Patin, since there seems to be no role for low tone in the language, a privative analysis is pursued. That is, it is assumed that all syllables are phonologically either H-toned or toneless... Specifically, all words in Saghala carry at most one H.... The default pattern in Saghala is the following: The two syllables following a sponsor receive high tone, while the sponsor itself is low-toned at the surface." Breteler says nothing about stress in Saghala and reports no acoustic study (2.5.1, p.52: "further research is warranted to determine if the proposed foot structure is reflected in the acoustics of Saghala"). So the modern source neither confirms nor denies Wray's penultimate accent; tone and penultimate prominence plausibly coexist (as in neighbouring NE-coast Bantu), and Wray's tense-specific 'final accent' in the immediate future is very likely a grammatical (melodic) H rather than a stress shift. Patin 2009 itself is paywalled…

When a suffix is used the accent is moved so as to be on the last syllable but one. There are but few monosyllabic words in the Sagalla dialect." These when pronounced together form one word, as — Ni-je-m-kwita, I will beat him. Wa-m-tag-ile, they have sold him" (pp.42-43), with the order "subjective personal prefix... tense prefix... objective prefix" before the root (p.43) — i.e. a typically Bantu profile: inflection (class/number, subject, object, tense, negation) overwhelmingly prefixal, derivation…

evidence_works.work: Woidich 1974, Ein arabischer Bauerndialekt aus dem südlichen Oberägypten (Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft 124: 42-58)
evidence_works.note: Gives the same three-step weight rule as the entry's Khalafallah 1969 rule for a third Sa'idi locality: (1) a long vowel takes the accent (dilgē, bētak); (2) otherwise the vowel immediately before the consonant cluster nearest the word end (masákt, zágla, ʿískiri, ḥaggigílna); (3) otherwise the accent moves forward to the vowel nearest the word beginning or a morpheme boundary (mára, il+mára, mázag, it+mázag, it+mízigat, nit+kíri). Refinements beyond the entry: the explicit 'or a morpheme boundary' clause of rule 3, under which the article il+ and verbal prefix it+/nit+ stand outside the stressed stem (parallel to the entry's sec. 2.3.6 point that assimilated article/prefix geminates do not affect stress); and sec. 2.2.2, where apparent exceptions (búguṛti 'my cow', núḍurta 'she saw him', líbista 'she put it on', ṭúrruzta 'she embroidered it', naxaḷti 'my date palm', núrubṭu 'we bind', ǧázimti 'my shoe', iǧḥá 'Guha': stress printed on the first syllable, where surface rule 2 would put it before the final cluster) are derived by applying the stress rules to underlying forms (+buguṛati, +nuḍurata, +libsata, +ṭurruzata, +naxaḷati, +nurbuṭu, +ǧazmati, +ǧḥa) before feminine -a elision and epenthesis, so stress is not re-assigned after elision. One variable item: yíštiri ~ yištíri 'he buys' both attested in texts and recordings, but always ištára; the like-structured yištiki 'he complains' and yistiḥi 'he is ashamed' are always stressed on the first syllable. No secondary-stress statement; no phrase-level stress statement (the paper's only stress passage is secs. 2.2.1-2.2.2). Coding unchanged: kind=weight, domain WORD, exn 0.

1618.dloc: Gruzdeva 1997 §2.1.2, paragraph beginning 'Ударение разноместное и подвижное'; Fortescue 2016 Introduction p. 6, paragraph beginning 'Stress in simplex words'
1618.prule: Nivkh word stress (Gruzdeva 1997, pan-Nivkh description citing an explicit East Sakhalin form): 'raznomestnoe i podvizhnoe' = free (not bound to a fixed syllable) and mobile, and can be meaning-distinguishing (ҳáунт 'names' vs ҳаýнт 'dries'); the same word may be stressed differently across dialects, e.g. Amur ámamd' vs East Sakhalin amámnt 'walks'. Fortescue 2016 relaying Krejnovic 1979: 298: ES stress 'mobile', e.g. bisyllabic transitives stressed on the 2nd syllable vs intransitives on the 1st, and ES lacks the Amur retraction of stress to the initial syllable. No fixed or weight-computable position is stated for ES.
1618.srule: Not mentioned in Gruzdeva 1997 §2.1.2 (whole phonology section 2.1.0-2.1.4 read) nor in Fortescue 2016 Introduction p. 6: both treat only the position of the (single) word stress, always-stressed affixes and compound stress.

morph.rootq: "Stress accent is quite noticeable in Salinan, and appears to be inherent in the roots and particles and inexplicable by any rules. Frequently, however, a word bears primary and secondary stress accents of nearly equal force which may be confused." (p.9, Accent). Affix-specific remarks elsewhere: "The suffix -o of the third person generally takes the stress accent and stems ending in -o distinguish their third personal possessives by this method alone" (p.30); "the first personal plural possessive form is equivalent to the first personal singular form plus the prefix ta. The accent generally falls on this prefix" (p.31); proclitics "are never found independently and may carry the accent"…
morph.elicq: No statement ties the stress description to a particular elicitation mode. Closest context: "Naturally this harsh character is far more evident when the words are given slowly with the careful enunciation inevitable to the recording of native language. In rapid speech much of this harshness ... is softened." (p.7); "During this time Dr. T. T. Waterman made some researches on the phonetics of the language with the help of various mechanical apparatus" (p.4; kymograph and palatogram results are cited for consonants and vowels, pp.7-12, not for stress). Stress marks are written on both vocabulary items and the dictated connected texts (pp.60-120).
morph.stmt: Mixed, with the major grammatical categories prefixed and the minor/derivational ones suffixed: "The various morphological processes are accomplished by means of prefixes, suffixes, and infixes" (p.18); "The verbal stem is modified by prefixes, infixes, and suffixes, to a lesser extent by the affixation of enclitics and proclitics. The infixes are concerned exclusively with pluralization...; the prefixes express the principal modal qualifications, the suffixes the lesser ones" (p.34); for nouns "practically all other etymological elements are suffixed" apart from nominal t- (p.29), with 1st/2nd-person possessors prefixed and 3rd-person suffixed (p.30), object pronouns suffixed (p.46) and…

1624.dq: The basic primary stress pattern of Samoan is simple: a moraic trochee at the right edge of the word (Homer 2007a). Stress is on the last vowel if long, and otherwise on the second-to-last.
1624.dloc: Zuraw et al. 2014 sec. 3.1 'Primary stress in monomorphemes' (ms p. 6; publ. ~p. 281) and sec. 7.1; Pratt 1893 Grammar pp. 2-3
1624.heavy: long vowel (V:) in the final syllable attracts stress; diphthongising VV sequences ai/au/ei/ou also form the bimoraic foot head (Pratt: 'words ending in a long vowel... all words ending in a diphthong' take ultima accent). All syllables open, so no CVC.
1624.prule: Moraic trochee at the right word edge: primary stress on the final syllable if its vowel is long (or the word ends in a diphthongising VV: ai, au, ei, ou), otherwise on the penultimate syllable (= penultimate mora).
1624.srule: Secondary stresses on the heads of additional bimoraic trochees before the final (primary) foot: non-final long vowels are stressed ((mà:)(lò:)(ló:) 'rest'); 4-mora words stress the first mora ((vào)(váo), (sàva)(lí-a)); in 5-mora words (mostly loans) the word begins with a foot, so secondary stress is on the first mora, not the second ((tèmo)ka(lási), *te(mòka)(lási): 'initial dactyl effect'), except that an epenthetic first vowel pushes it to the second (pa(làni)(kéke)); medial-foot alignment in longer words undetermined (only (ʔàfa)(kàni)si(tána)); the authors call the initial-foot analysis tentative.

1625.heavy: CVV and CVG (syllable closed by the left leg of a geminate) heaviest; final superheavy CVVC/CVCC next; CVC heavy only non-finally and within the last three syllables; CV light
1625.dflt: leftmost CV (light) syllable: initial in 'katab, 'darasat, 'ragabatih, but second-syllable in mak'tabatī 'my library', where the initial CVC is pre-antepenultimate and skipped (p. 82)
1625.prule: Weight hierarchy CVV/CVG (G = left leg of geminate) > final superheavy CVVC/CVCC > CVC > CV: (a) rightmost non-final CVV/CVG syllable, unbounded (even pre-antepenultimate, e.g. musajjilatī); (b) else a final CVVC/CVCC; (c) else rightmost non-final CVC within the last three syllables; (d) else leftmost CV syllable; (e) final CVV stressed in disyllabic adjectives and di-/trisyllabic imperfect verbs. Preceded (p.81) by the generic peninsular algorithm (3): final superheavy > rightmost non-final heavy up to antepenult > leftmost light, which 'holds for stress assignment in most types of words in San'ani' but is then revised to (8).
1625.srule: Secondary stress present (unlike Cairene) in words of two or more binary moraic-trochee feet: heads of feet not bearing main stress carry secondary stress. Two-foot words follow foot construction: final CVVC + non-final CVV/CVG -> main on one heavy, secondary on the other, order set by optional foot extrametricality (xā.ri.jīn); CVC + penultimate CVV -> main on the CVV, secondary on the CVC (yiḏbaḥūhin); two light-light feet -> S w s w (katabatih: main initial, secondary penult), reversed to s w S w when foot extrametricality fails. Four-foot words: a rhythmic layer alternates feet (mustašfayāt: primary on the final foot, secondary on the penultimate foot; tiliviziyūnāt: secondary on the leftmost foot head when primary is on the penultimate foot, on the antepenultimate foot when primary is final).

1629.prule: Stress usually on the final syllable of the word (quantity-insensitive; loanwords also final). 1630.heavy: Where a double vowel nucleus occurs in a bisyllabic word, the stress usually falls on it. (minor weight element; main conditioning is vowel quality, not weight)
1630.prule: Stress placement conditioned by a vowel-strength (sonority) hierarchy a > i > u > o > ɛ: the stronger vowel tends to take primary stress; with identical vowels the first is stressed; editor's generalisation: in word-final VCV(CV)# the first syllable of that sequence takes primary stress unless the second has a stronger vowel (covers >80% of forms). Trisyllables: medial, or initial (+final secondary); quadrisyllables: 2nd (+final secondary) or 3rd (+initial secondary); five-syllable words: 4th (+2nd secondary). No minimal pairs; author calls phonemic status of stress uncertain.
1630.srule: Secondary stress on alternate syllables both preceding and following the primary-stressed syllable (volume editor's fn. 2). In the author's transcriptions a non-affixed word carries at most one secondary: bisyllables with initial primary on the 2nd syllable; trisyllables with initial primary on the final; quadrisyllables primary 2nd + secondary 4th, or primary 3rd + secondary 1st; five-syllable words primary 4th + secondary 2nd; medial-stressed trisyllables and final-stressed bisyllables have none.

dqtr.text: Popoloca prosodic stress, unlike that of Spanish, is manifested by the lengthening of the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word or of one of the consonants of the last syllable, without affecting the intensity or the pitch of the latter.

1631.dq: El acento prosódico popoloca, a diferencia del español, se manifiesta por la prolongación de la vocal de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra o de una de las consonantes de la última sílaba, sin afectar la intensidad ni el tono de ésta.
1631.dloc: Diccionario 1995, Gramatica sec. 0.3-0.3.3, pp. 293-295 (pp. 314-316 of the SIL facsimile); K&P 1968 p. 25 sec. 4.2
1631.prule: Accent (realized as segment lengthening, not intensity or pitch) is anchored to the last syllable of the ROOT: most words have 'consonantal accent' = lengthening of the (simple, or glottal/n member of a cluster) onset consonant of the root-final syllable; some words instead have 'vocalic accent' = lengthening of the vowel of the penultimate syllable (obligatory when the root-final syllable begins with a vowel or y/v, otherwise lexically contrastive with the consonantal type). Tonic suffixes (-na 1st person authority, negative -hya, diminutives -xjan, -ntsi) take the accent and the root accent is suppressed; atonic suffixes (e.g. -ni, cf. dictionary transcription tsjacani [tsjaa'ca'ni]) leave it on the root. Source states accent is predictable for the great majority of words with minimal exceptions.
1631.quote: El acento prosódico popoloca, a diferencia del español, se manifiesta por la prolongación de la vocal de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra o de una de las consonantes de la última sílaba, sin afectar la intensidad ni el tono de ésta. La acentuación de la gran mayoría de las palabras se puede predecir, y el número de excepciones es mínimo. 0.3.1. El acento vocálico. En algunas palabras se acentúa la vocal de la penúltima sílaba. La vocal acentuada tiene una duración prolongada. Si la última sílaba de la raíz empieza con vocal o con y o v, la vocal de la penúltima sílaba siempre es prolongada. …

tn.quote: El popoloca es un idioma tonal; cada sílaba de cada palabra tiene un tono musical con significado. Hay cuatro tonos sencillos en el popoloca de San Juan Atzingo, y además hay algunos contornos de tono en una sola sílaba. Un contorno tonal empieza con un tono y termina con otro. ... Los cuatro niveles de tono están indicados con números en la ortografía fonética: el tono más agudo es 1, el tono más bajo 4, el tono medio agudo es 2 y el medio bajo es 3. También hay grupos tonales que tienen un movimiento de un nivel tonal a otro en la misma sílaba ...
tn.translation: Popoloca is a tonal language; every syllable of every word has a meaningful musical pitch (tone). There are four simple tones in San Juan Atzingo Popoloca, and in addition there are some tone contours on a single syllable. A tonal contour begins with one tone and ends with another. ... The four tone levels are indicated with numbers in the phonetic orthography: the highest tone is 1, the lowest tone 4, the mid-high tone is 2 and the mid-low is 3. 1633.dq: It is upon the first syllable of the stem that the accent falls, not upon the first syllable of the word; prefixes, therefore, do not affect the question.
1633.prule: Main accent on the first syllable of the STEM (prefixes not counted; disyllables prefix+stem are thus final-accented); secondary weaker accent on the penult when more than two syllables follow the stem-initial syllable; a slight accent on the first of two or more verbal prefix syllables.
1633.srule: Secondary (weaker) accent on the penult when more than two syllables follow the stem-initial main accent; in verbs with two or more prefix syllables the first prefix syllable also takes a slight accent. Non-iterative.
1633.quote: The accent in Kongo falls upon the first syllable of the stem. When more than two syllables follow the first syllable of the stem, a secondary and weaker accent falls upon the penult. It is upon the first syllable of the stem that the accent falls, not upon the first syllable of the word; prefixes, therefore, do not affect the question. If a verb possesses prefixes to the extent of two or more syllables, the first of such prefix-syllables receives also a slight accent. ... Dissyllabic words are accented on their last syllable according to the foregoing rule. ... In the case of maki, meso, din…
1633.idn: Bentley 1887 describes Kongo 'as spoken at San Salvador' (Mbanza Kongo, northern Angola), i.e. Kisikongo. Glottolog's bibliography tags this work 'Southern variety around Mbanza Kongo = Kisikongo = Koongo [kng]' (ref 39095), and Kisikongo [kisi1245] is a Glottolog dialect of South-Central Koongo [koon1244] > Southern…

The perfect of the applied form of the verb, in both the active and passive voices, requires strong accentuation on the penult. ... The few words ending in enia and ania take the accent on the penult ... A few …
1633.tone: Bentley (1887) describes 'accent' only and never tone; separately he notes 'a special prolongation of utterance' distinguishing a very few minimal pairs (baka 'catch' vs baka 'rend'; nkaka 'manis' vs nkaka 'grandparent'). Modern check: Dom & Bostoen 2020 (JHL 10(2), Kisikongo present-future isomorphism), fn. 13: 'Because Bentley (1887) neither discusses tone patterns nor writes tone on Kisikongo examples, we cannot determine whether the constructions had identical or different tone patterns.' From Ndonga Mfuwa (1995) data the same paper treats present-day Kisikongo as tonal and hypothesises, with an explicit hedge ('This hypothesis is of course in need of further corroboration'), that future/simple-present verbs carry 'a high tone on the root vowel which undergoes rightward spread to the next syllable or any other syllable that is not word-final' (okóta, otú:nga, osónéka), i.e. root-initial H. It states no stress rule and does not deny stress. Bentley's stem-initial 'accent' plausibly registers the root-initial H of a tone system; the dedicated modern prosodic description (Ndonga Mfuwa 1995, Systematique grammaticale du kisikongo) was not reachable, so no reachable primary contradicts Bentley's accent rule and the verdict stays set by morphology with this caveat.

dqtr.text: In other Quechua dialects, stress is predictable and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, that is, it does not have phonological status. By contrast, in the santiagueña [Santiago del Estero] variety, stress is phonological since it is not predictable.

1634.dq: En otros dialectos quechuas, el acento es predecible y recae sobre la penúltima sílaba de la palabra, es decir, no tiene rango fonológico. En cambio, en la variedad santiagueña, el acento es fonológico pues no es predictible.
1634.prule: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable ('En la inmensa mayoría de los casos cae en la penúltima sílaba'); the default is productive -- Spanish loans with final or antepenultimate stress are automatically re-accented to penultimate ('palabras agudas y esdrújulas se tornan graves: [sandía] > [sándia]'). A bounded set of words carries final stress: two native nouns cited (punchaw [punčáw] 'día', qollur [qožúr] 'estrella fugaz'), loans from other indigenous languages and some hispanisms (paragwáy, taŋgól, karáŋ, simból, 'etc.'), and apocope forms where loss of a suffix leaves the formerly penultimate stress word-final (-spa > -s: [purís] < [purispa]; dropped topicalizer -qa: [warmé] < [warmiqa]), the final stress there marking a zero-grade suffix.

morph.elicq: No statement of the evidential basis for the accent description is given in Cap. II (Fonología); the section simply asserts 'En la inmensa mayoría de los casos cae en la penúltima sílaba' with isolated citation forms ([punčáw] 'día', [paragwáy], [sándia] < sandía) and refers to Cerrón-Palomino (1987) and Nardi (1987) for detail ('Estos aspectos han sido tratados en detalle por Cerrón-Palomino (1987: 245); también puede consultarse Nardi (1987:15)'). Elsewhere the grammar mentions 'nuestros informantes' (Cap. IV n.5) but not in connection with stress.
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'El quechua es una lengua aglutinante en la que la raíz presenta uno o más afijos. Su morfología funciona mediante un único tipo de afijos: los sufijos, es decir, no admite prefijos ni infijos' (Alderetes Cap. V, Introducción); enclitics 'ocupan las posiciones más externas respecto del tema, cerrando la estructura de la palabra' (Cap. IV p.6); Juanatey 2024 p.290: 'Presenta morfología aglutinante y sufijante'. The only preposed grammatical material is free particles (mana/ama NEG, suk, kay/chay determiners).

secx.sec_quote_tr: In other Quechua dialects the accent is predictable and falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, i.e. it has no phonological status. By contrast, in the Santiago del Estero variety the accent is phonological, since it is not predictable. [The whole 'EL ACENTO' section speaks of one accent per word (penult vs. final) and never mentions secondary, rhythmic or alternating stress.]
